W.prompt: Dylan exercises every 12 days and Karen every 8 days. When will they next exercise together — is this a GCF problem or an LCM problem?
W.explanation: They meet again in the future, so it is the LCM.
W.tip: LCM: meeting again in the future; key words least, next, lowest. GCF: splitting into equal groups; key words greatest, most, highest.

W.prompt: Dylan exercises every 12 days and Karen every 8 days. If they both exercised today, how many days until they exercise together again?
W.explanation: Multiples of 12: 12, 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. They meet on day 24.

W.prompt: Mrs. Miller splits 112 roses, 64 daisies and 48 orchids into identical vases — is this a GCF problem or an LCM problem?
W.explanation: She is splitting flowers into equal groups, so it is the GCF.
W.tip: LCM: meeting again in the future; key words least, next, lowest. GCF: splitting into equal groups; key words greatest, most, highest.

W.prompt: Mrs. Miller has 112 roses, 64 daisies and 48 orchids to split into identical vases with none left over. What is the largest number of vases she can make?
W.explanation: The GCF of 112, 64 and 48 is 16, so she can make 16 vases.

W.prompt: Mrs. Miller makes 16 identical vases from 112 roses, 64 daisies and 48 orchids. How many roses go in each vase?
W.explanation: 112 ÷ 16 = 7 roses. (And 64 ÷ 16 = 4 daisies, 48 ÷ 16 = 3 orchids.)

W.prompt: Mrs. Miller makes 16 identical vases from 112 roses, 64 daisies and 48 orchids. How many daisies go in each vase?
W.explanation: 64 ÷ 16 = 4 daisies.

W.prompt: Mrs. Miller makes 16 identical vases from 112 roses, 64 daisies and 48 orchids. How many orchids go in each vase?
W.explanation: 48 ÷ 16 = 3 orchids.

W.prompt: Hot dogs come in packs of 8 and hamburgers in packs of 10, and Mr. Jones wants the same number of each — is this a GCF problem or an LCM problem?
W.explanation: Be careful! It sounds like splitting, but he needs a number both packs can reach — the LCM.
W.tip: LCM: meeting again in the future; key words least, next, lowest. GCF: splitting into equal groups; key words greatest, most, highest.

W.prompt: Mr. Jones wants the same number of hot dogs and hamburgers. Hot dogs come in packs of 8, hamburgers in packs of 10. What is the smallest number of each he can buy?
W.explanation: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40. The LCM is 40 — that is 5 packs of hot dogs and 4 packs of hamburgers.

W.prompt: Stephanie fills identical party bags with 18 bouncy balls, 108 candies and 45 stickers — is this a GCF problem or an LCM problem?
W.explanation: She is splitting things into equal bags, so it is the GCF.
W.tip: LCM: meeting again in the future; key words least, next, lowest. GCF: splitting into equal groups; key words greatest, most, highest.

W.prompt: Stephanie has 18 bouncy balls, 108 pieces of candy and 45 stickers. What is the largest number of identical bags she can make?
W.explanation: The GCF of 18, 108 and 45 is 9. Each bag gets 2 balls, 12 candies and 5 stickers.

W.prompt: Stephanie makes 9 identical bags from 108 pieces of candy. How many candies are in each bag?
W.explanation: 108 ÷ 9 = 12 candies in each bag.

W.prompt: There are 40 girls and 32 boys. Every soccer team must have the same number of girls and the same number of boys. What is the greatest number of teams they can make?
W.explanation: The GCF of 40 and 32 is 8, so there are 8 teams — the most teams means the fewest players on each.

W.prompt: 40 girls and 32 boys are split into 8 identical teams. How many boys are on each team?
W.explanation: 32 ÷ 8 = 4 boys on each team (and 40 ÷ 8 = 5 girls).

W.prompt: Every 100th caller wins $100 and every 20th caller wins a concert ticket. Which caller wins both — is this a GCF problem or an LCM problem?
W.explanation: Two patterns meeting at a caller further on — that is the LCM.
W.tip: LCM: meeting again in the future; key words least, next, lowest. GCF: splitting into equal groups; key words greatest, most, highest.

W.prompt: A radio station gives $100 to every 100th caller and a concert ticket to every 20th caller. Which caller is the first to get both prizes?
W.explanation: Every multiple of 100 is also a multiple of 20, so the 100th caller gets both.

W.prompt: A reader’s club has 12 hardbacks, 18 paperbacks and 36 magazines. Each set is shared equally among the members. What is the greatest possible number of members?
W.explanation: The GCF of 12, 18 and 36 is 6.

W.prompt: Three video game villains appear every 5, 10 and 16 seconds. When do all three appear together — is this a GCF problem or an LCM problem?
W.explanation: They meet again later in time, so it is the LCM.
W.tip: LCM: meeting again in the future; key words least, next, lowest. GCF: splitting into equal groups; key words greatest, most, highest.

W.prompt: One villain appears every 5 seconds, a second every 10 seconds and a third every 16 seconds. How many seconds pass between the times all three appear together?
W.explanation: Be careful — 5 does not go into 16, so you cannot divide all three by 5. LCM of 5 and 10 is 10; LCM of 10 and 16 is 80. They meet every 80 seconds.
W.hint: With three numbers, find the LCM of two of them first, then of that answer and the third.

W.prompt: Emily has 6 angel fish, 12 tiger barbs and 15 guppies. Every tank must hold the same number of each kind. What is the greatest number of tanks she can set up?
W.explanation: The GCF of 6, 12 and 15 is 3. Each tank gets 2 angel fish, 4 tiger barbs and 5 guppies.

K.prompt: The GCF of two numbers can be bigger than both numbers.
K.explanation: A factor of a number is never bigger than the number, so the GCF is always less than or equal to the numbers.

K.prompt: The LCM of two numbers is always greater than or equal to both numbers.
K.explanation: Multiples start at the number itself and grow, so the LCM can never be smaller than either number.

K.prompt: If two numbers share no factor except 1, their LCM is the two numbers multiplied together.
K.explanation: For example 5 and 7 share only 1, and their LCM is 5 × 7 = 35.
1 is a factor of every number, so the GCF is at least 1. For 9 and 17 it is exactly 1.

K.prompt: Match each key word to the kind of problem.
K.explanation: Greatest, most and splitting into groups point to the GCF. Least, next and meeting again point to the LCM.

K.prompt: Which shows 54 + 36 with the GREATEST common factor taken out?
K.explanation: The GCF of 54 and 36 is 18: 54 + 36 = 18(3 + 2). 6(9 + 6) and 9(6 + 4) are equal too, but the numbers left inside still share a factor.

K.prompt: Put the ladder-method steps for the LCM in order.
K.explanation: Divide by shared factors, stop when the bottom row shares nothing, then multiply the side and the bottom (the L).
items: Divide both numbers by a factor they share
Keep going until the bottom numbers share only 1
Multiply the side numbers and the bottom numbers together
